summary: Defines a binding for the JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP) over WebSocket. It provides better performance than the HTTP binding for JMAP. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: JMAP is a way for email programs to talk to mail servers. This document lets them keep one open line, like a phone call, so the talking is quicker than sending many separate letters.

questions: how to run jmap over websocket
how does jmap authenticate over websocket
what is the jmap websocket subprotocol
how do jmap push notifications work
subtitle: How JMAP clients and servers can keep one authenticated WebSocket open instead of authenticating every HTTP request.

tldr.problem: JMAP over HTTP requires every API request to be authenticated, which can be expensive in time and resources, and HTTP requests are rarely compressed.
tldr.mechanism: The client authenticates once while opening a WebSocket with the subprotocol name jmap, then sends JMAP requests as JSON text frames and receives responses and optional push notifications on the same connection.
tldr.outcome: Authentication happens only on the handshake and the credentials stay in effect for the life of the connection. Compression can be negotiated, and servers can push state changes to the client.

today: RFC 8887 is a Proposed Standard from August 2020, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the core protocol in RFC 8620.

sections.title: Why a WebSocket Binding
sections.content:
The JSON Meta Application Protocol (JMAP, RFC 8620) normally runs over HTTP, and every JMAP API request must be authenticated. Depending on the authentication type and the server configuration, that can be an expensive operation in both time and resources, so reauthenticating each request may harm performance.

The WebSocket binding (RFC 6455) authenticates only the handshake request. Those credentials then stay in effect for the whole connection. The binding carries JMAP API requests and responses, with optional support for push notifications.

It can also optionally compress both requests and responses using RFC 7692. The RFC notes that compressing HTTP responses is ubiquitous, but compressing HTTP requests has very low, if any, deployment, so it is not a viable option for JMAP API requests over HTTP.
sections.eli5: Showing your ID once and then keeping the line open is faster than showing it for every single question.

sections.title: Discovering WebSocket Support
sections.content:
A client finds out whether a server offers this binding from the JMAP Session object. Servers that support it MUST add a capability named urn:ietf:params:jmap:websocket to the capabilities object. Its value is an object with two properties.

  • url: the wss URI to use when starting the JMAP-over-WebSocket handshake.
  • supportsPush: a boolean that is true if the server supports push notifications over the WebSocket.
sections.eli5: The server's welcome sheet says whether it has a phone line and what the number is.

sections.title: Handshake and Authentication
sections.content:
The client and server agree to use the WebSocket JMAP subprotocol during the normal WebSocket handshake. That handshake can be an HTTP/1.1 Upgrade request (RFC 6455) or an HTTP/2 Extended CONNECT request (RFC 8441). The subprotocol is also intended for future HTTP bindings such as HTTP/3, provided a WebSocket handshake is defined for them.

The client MUST first do a TLS handshake on a wss:// URL, and MUST close the connection if that fails. It then makes an authenticated HTTP request on the encrypted connection and MUST include jmap in the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header field. The server's reply MUST carry the same header with the value jmap, or no JMAP connection is established.

The credentials in that first request remain in effect for the whole connection. If they expire, the server can treat later requests as unauthenticated or close the connection, optionally with a Close frame carrying status code 1008 (Policy Violation). After the handshake, other message types MUST NOT be sent over the connection.
sections.eli5: You say the secret password word, jmap, and show your ID once. If both sides agree, the line stays open and only JMAP talk is allowed on it.

sections.title: Messages: Requests, Responses and Errors
sections.content:
Data messages MUST be text frames holding UTF-8. Each message is a single JSON object. A client sends a JMAP Request, a WebSocketPushEnable or a WebSocketPushDisable object. A server sends a Response, a JSON Problem Details object or a StateChange object. Fragmented WebSocket messages MUST be coalesced before they are parsed as JSON.

The binding adds fields to the core JMAP objects.

  • Request gets @type (always Request) and an optional client-chosen id.
  • Response gets @type (always Response) and requestId, which MUST be returned if the request had an id.
  • Request-level errors use a Problem Details object with @type set to RequestError and the same requestId rule.

The server may process requests out of order, so the id is how a client matches responses to requests. The maxConcurrentRequests limit also applies on the WebSocket, and over a multiplexing HTTP binding such as HTTP/2 it applies to the sum of requests on the API endpoint and the WebSocket.

A server MUST return a Problem Details object for request-level errors such as an invalid JMAP object, an unsupported capability or method call, or exceeding a server request limit. If an endpoint receives a binary frame, it can ignore it or close the connection, optionally with status code 1003 (Unsupported Data). If a client gets a message of an unexpected form, it can ignore it or close, optionally with status code 1007 (Invalid frame payload data).
sections.eli5: Every message is a note in a standard format. You can write a number on your note, and the answer repeats that number so you know which question it belongs to.

sections.title: Push Notifications
sections.content:
A server that supports push advertises supportsPush: true in its WebSocket capability. Push notifications are standard JMAP StateChange objects, with one extra optional field: pushState. This is a preferably short string that encodes the entire server state visible to the user, not just the objects in that call.

The point of pushState is to let a client catch up immediately on anything that changed while it was disconnected. Without it, a client has to issue a series of /changes requests after reconnecting.

A client turns push on by sending a WebSocketPushEnable object. Its dataTypes property lists the data type names of interest, such as Mailbox or Email, or is null for all supported types. Its optional pushState property carries the last token the client received, and the server SHOULD then immediately send all changes since that state. A client turns push off for the connection by sending a WebSocketPushDisable object.
sections.eli5: You can ask the server to tap you on the shoulder when your mail changes. If you were away, you tell it the last thing you knew, and it catches you up.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of both WebSocket (RFC 6455) and JMAP (RFC 8620) apply. To protect confidentiality and integrity, the connection MUST use TLS 1.2 or later, following the recommendations of BCP 195 (RFC 7525). Servers SHOULD support TLS 1.3 or later.

The binding can be used by clients inside and outside a web browser, so the relevant WebSocket considerations in RFC 6455 apply to each environment.

IANA has registered the subprotocol identifier jmap, with the common name WebSocket Transport for JMAP (JSON Meta Application Protocol), in the WebSocket Subprotocol Name Registry.
sections.eli5: The phone line must be a scrambled, private one, and the special name jmap has been officially written in the list of allowed names.
